Insufficient snapshot/identity workspace, or old unreserved history that cannot be normalized after upgrade, raises JOURNAL WORKSPACE REQUIRES QUOTA PLAN . Source snapshots are currently all built before delivery; streaming reclamation across a large table, partial snapshot rebasing and oversized-transaction staging are unfinished. Expand capacity or use an explicit plan; never delete journal parts to make room. Quota is excluded from semantic identity: stop affected workers, change/reload configuration, then resume with the current global error generation. See configuration revisions for supported console changes. Journal choices LOCAL uses Java-8-compatible H2 2.2.224. path is a private directory, relative to the configuration file; it contains sensitive rows and receives mode 0700. Automatic server mode allows same-host CLI status/resume. It is not a cross-host database service. Preserve the whole directory/volume; do not copy a live .mv.db alone. Use EXTERNAL for cross-host takeover; shared-filesystem H2 has not been accepted as a cluster journal. EXTERNAL supports PostgreSQL, openGauss or a separate MySQL instance. Workers share journal instance/namespace/pipelineId and target configuration, with distinct nodeIds. Database-clock leases and epochs fence ownership. MySQL storage must use InnoDB and retain acknowledged commits across restart. External HA systems promote/fence database nodes; Rivomesh does not promote them. V3 worker-crash recovery, MySQL 8.4 async promotion and MGR election during snapshot passed; other versions/soak matrices still need acceptance. V2 results do not prove all V3 variants. Troubleshooting and FAQ - SQL errors: only that subscriber pauses with an error generation. Repair privileges/schema/data, then resume the original transaction using the current generation from status . Resume never skips data or edits GTIDs. - Connection loss/deadlocks: transient errors retry; local destination fencing blocks stale owners. Source reconnect validates candidate GTIDs and snapshot dependencies. Missing logs/multiple writers block or wait without rewinding progress. - Journal quota: CDC backlog uses the backpressure/recovery path above; snapshots or indivisible oversized commits need capacity/error-generation plans. Budget snapshot/identity copies, normalization reservation and the backlog window. Backpressure cannot reconstruct permanently lost storage or source binlogs purged before they were read. - Live DDL: currently blocks safely, including potentially unrelated-database SQL that could reference selected objects. Historical DDL evolution and explicit skip plans are unfinished. - UNIQUE(email): DOWNGRADE BUSINESS creates an ordinary secondary index. Source constraints, exclusive sync writes and transactional/idempotent checkpoints jointly preserve source uniqueness. Validate and restore constraints before application writes. Primary, identity and internal keys are never downgraded. - GSI: business GSI model entries can become ordinary indexes, losing global routing/uniqueness. Identity GSIs require a distribution plan. Existing GSIs/unique constraints are never blindly dropped. Commercial distributed GaussDB is not hardware-validated. - Expression/prefix/descending/special indexes: require a separate plan; the target pauses instead of silently omitting them. Unsupported indexes block before creating a missing table. - Types: common integers/unsigned, decimal/floating point, text/binary, YEAR, DATE/DATETIME/TIMESTAMP and JSON are covered. V3 now implements signed microsecond MySQL TIME durations with matching JDBC snapshot and TIME/TIME2 row-event text. Relational targets use INTERVAL/MySQL TIME(6); analytical/event targets retain duration text. See the Kingbase guide and DM guide for first native acceptance scope. BIT, ENUM/SET, spatial/zero dates, non-InnoDB and other objects need extension/testing. - V2 migration: continue the old configuration to retain v2 checkpoints. Adding formatVersion: 3 cannot take over a populated old target. Explicit data/state migration planning remains necessary. Replace 1 with the relevant subscriber or pipeline error generation. Stale requests are rejected. Permanent source errors persist as ERROR and block standby claims; pause reports each fence confirmation. RBAC/local accounts/configuration editing/audit are implemented. See implementation status for scoped recovery. LOCAL connection lifetime and controller memory The controller retains a stable connection to each opened LOCAL journal, including paused/stopped tasks, until configuration replacement or controller shutdown. On restart it opens existing files; inspecting a never-started task does not create its journal. Same-host CLI/certificate/repair operations therefore share a stable H2 automatic-server endpoint. Each opened journal has a 4 MiB page-cache setting plus schema/index metadata and connection-thread overhead. Worker heaps, control-store connections and IAM/audit state consume additional memory. Docker/Linux/Helm controller defaults now use a 512 MiB maximum heap; Helm exposes controllerHeapMiB . Size by initialized LOCAL journal count, schema volume and measured heap use; maxTasks limits task count. External transactional journals are available for larger installations. Optional protocol5 adds administrator evidence creation,raw/normalized pages and typed image review. See review operations for activation/upgrade and deployment profiles. Default legacy profiles do not upgrade automatically. See implementation status for scoped recovery.

title: Platform design
text: Rivomesh complete product and technical design Updated: 2026-11-15. 中文：完整方案. See requirements for decisions and status. This is the full design, not a claim that every feature is complete. V3 now supports multiple explicitly mapped databases within one logical MySQL source, fan-out, multiple configurations with isolated workers, optional durable journals and Web management. The v2 single-database/single-target mode remains compatible. See implementation status and validation for each adapter's accepted scope, and the console manual for operations. Remaining capabilities follow the phases below. 1. Product and scope Rivomesh serves enterprise/government database migration, continuous replication, data distribution, validation, and cutover orchestration. A bilingual Web workbench guides ordinary installations; configuration files, APIs, and CLI use the same model for experts. Dimension Scope --- --- Current delivery source MySQL, including existing 8.0/8.4 coverage; standalone, GTID replication, single-primary MGR Future sources PostgreSQL and Oracle; design Source SPI and neutral event/position models now, without claiming available connectors Relational targets MySQL, PostgreSQL, openGauss, distributed GaussDB, DM, Kingbase, OceanBase, GBase; profile product/version/mode/engine separately Analytics/warehouse targets ClickHouse, Apache Doris, Apache Hive; classify GBase analytical/transactional variants by actual capabilities Current delivery message targets Kafka, Pulsar, RabbitMQ, RocketMQ, ActiveMQ (separate Classic/Artemis profiles), Redis Streams, NATS JetStream Deployment Linux manual, Docker, Kubernetes Helm, native Kubernetes manifests Storage Local durable journal, eligible target-hosted journal, independent shared journal Broad version coverage means an expanding compatibility matrix and capability detection, not unconditional support for every historical release/fork/combination. Mark features verified/experimental/unverified/unsupported and identify actual products, versions, modes, drivers, hardware, and recovery boundaries. JDBC connectivity is insufficient acceptance evidence. 2. Multiple tasks and targets Each independent configuration defines one logical source, object selection, multiple targets, mappings, storage, and resource policy. Different configurations may connect to independent MySQL clusters. Support standalone task processes and a console managing isolated workers. Never implicitly merge sources into one transaction or destination table. Tasks, subscriptions, tables, targets, configuration revisions, and stream generations have independent identities. Candidate endpoints belong to one topology; database mappings are explicit. Preflight detects overlapping destination writers, replication loops, changed source identity, and fingerprint conflicts. New targets establish their own baselines. Isolate rate, connection/thread, memory, and disk quotas per task. Independent configurations capture separately by default. Explicit capture sharing may follow after validating privileges, filters, retention, source identity, and recovery dependencies, not merely matching hosts. Preserve cross-database transaction atomicity only within a target scope supporting it; no cross-target global XA. 3. Modules and contracts - Source SPI: discover capabilities/objects, create consistent baselines, capture transactions/DDL, encode/restore positions, validate failover, acknowledge upstream. GTID is not a universal source abstraction. - Journal SPI: persist complete transactions/large-transaction fragments, publish atomically, checksum, recover, enforce quotas, and reclaim. Advance safe capture only after durable completion. - Sink SPI: capability/object planning, write/publish, resolve uncertain commits, idempotency/versioning, DDL recovery, visibility. Model transactional writes, versioned materialization, batch publication, and messaging explicitly rather than assuming JDBC transactions everywhere. - Control/Worker: leases/fencing, isolation, configuration revisions, resource scheduling, and recoverable operation logs. Console outages must not destroy deployed worker checkpoints. - Validation/Cutover: baselines/barriers, differences, restored constraints, write ownership, and audit. Event envelopes carry logical sourceId, streamGeneration, transaction identity/ordinal, schemaVersion, table identity, operation, before/after, field-presence bitmap, snapshot/DDL/transaction boundaries, source position, and origin. IDs remain stable across retries and physical source failover; new baselines/lineages use new generations. Timestamps are observational, not ordering authorities. Positions are versioned typed payloads: MySQL GTID/dependencies, PostgreSQL LSN/slot/database/instance lineage, Oracle SCN/transaction/redo context, interpreted by their adapters. Do not compare them lexically or retain only the maximum observed SCN/LSN while losing open long transactions. Snapshot fragments also require stable IDs, completeness markers, and checkpoints. Future PostgreSQL capture must handle exported snapshots, slot/WAL retention, REPLICA IDENTITY, unchanged TOAST fields, and failover-slot readiness. Oracle requires supplemental logging, redo/archive coverage, long transactions, RAC/CDB/PDB, LOBs, and lineage. Official references describe readiness requirements for PG slots and supplemental logging for Oracle CDC. PostgreSQL, Oracle CDC reference. Review driver/capture distribution terms separately; future connectors are not existing failback channels. 4. Target capabilities and consistency Target class Write design Boundary shown in UI --- --- --- MySQL/PG/domestic transactional databases Dialect-specific batches or native upsert; local apply checkpoint commits with business data Source-transaction atomicity within supported target scope; central control storage does not replace the local checkpoint ClickHouse Stable materialization identity, monotonic version, delete markers; engine-specific replacement/read views Background ReplacingMergeTree merges do not guarantee deduplicated raw reads; validated FINAL/view contracts, no assumed cross-table transaction Doris Validated Unique Key/Merge-on-Write, sequence, deletes, Stream Load batch protocol Detect actual single/multi-table commit scope; resolve labels/txn state, timeouts, and retention windows per version Hive ACID capability mode or immutable file/partition/snapshot publication Ordinary tables are not row-oriented replicas; profile update/delete, visibility, transactions, and compaction Messaging Publish change events and transaction/snapshot boundaries with stable IDs Publisher confirmation is not downstream business completion; at-least-once by default, consumers must be idempotent ClickHouse replacement uses ORDER BY; mutable attributes or unstable partitioning cannot define row identity. Keep routing stable and coordinate old-version/tombstone cleanup with the oldest replayable position. Official engine guide. Doris Unique Key is a row-materialization model, distinct from a relaxable source business secondary UNIQUE. Do not mechanically replace it with Duplicate Key. Resolve lost acknowledgments against actual commit state; expired labels are not permanent deduplication evidence. Sequence columns, load transactions. These references do not guarantee every older version. Hive publication records batches, file manifests/digests, partitions, schemas, and metadata commit state. Readers must not see temporary files; object storage cannot be assumed to provide atomic rename. Recovery reconciles files/catalog to prevent duplicates, partial batches, and orphans. ACID mode instead uses validated transaction APIs/configuration and compaction. Hive Transactions. Analytical targets default to data-service/warehouse output, not unverified OLTP application takeover destinations. Expose captured (durably collected), delivered (accepted), applied/materialized, visible under the declared read contract, and validated at a barrier as supported. A single success indicator must not hide these differences. 5. No-PK tables, JSON, generated columns All three are first-release requirements needing development; current code rejects them. Removing validation does not implement support. Identity class Planned strategy --- --- Primary key Stable keyed scan/lookup, including key changes No PK but a reliable all-NOT-NULL unique candidate Validate semantics, use it as identity, handle changes; do not casually relax this identity constraint No unique key; identical duplicate rows allowed Consistent baseline, multiset semantics, durable technical identities/counts, exact before-image matching; each change modifies one occurrence A target auto-ID, unique whole-row hash, or online OFFSET cursor cannot solve keyless identity. Hashes only accelerate candidates; compare full typed values and preserve multiplicity. Never delete every equal row for one logged deletion. Added technical columns require explicit mappings/views and dependency checks; they cannot be claimed invisible to SELECT . Keyless snapshotting needs a replayable consistent artifact coordinated with the log baseline. Persist fragments/manifests before loading and replaying later transactions; deduplicate imports by fragment/transaction identity. If a source MVCC snapshot disappears with its connection, a row number cannot restore it. Resume completed artifacts or rebuild that table at a provable new baseline without resetting unrelated completed subscriptions. The same applies to failover during an unfinished keyless snapshot. Explain required coordination privileges, possible short locks/rescans, and disk costs; do not promise arbitrary keyless tables lock-free exact row-cursor recovery. MySQL row-search behavior is a design reference, not reused storage internals. JSON: decode MySQL binary JSON correctly, preserving numeric precision, SQL NULL versus JSON null, array ordering, and characters. Map to native JSON or text/LOB with declared query differences. Compare using documented semantic normalization rather than object-key ordering/whitespace. Initially require full JSON logging and retain empty binlog row value options unless partial-patch/historical-base recovery is implemented. MySQL JSON replication. Generated columns: distinguish STORED/VIRTUAL, actual logged presence/values, dependencies, and schema versions. Choose proven equivalent target expressions or ordinary-column materialization. Missing logged values require evaluation from historical inputs, never a later SELECT of the source's current row. Translation/evaluation covers SQL mode, collation, time zones, precision, and JSON functions; unsupported expressions produce precise blockers/alternatives, never silent NULLs. Do not INSERT explicit values into native target generated columns. Record takeover differences between materialized ordinary columns and native generation. MySQL generated columns. 6. DDL, existing targets, constraints Discover/version table definitions, indexes, expressions, and dependencies. Ordered DDL needs schema barriers and recoverable operation logs. Classify transformations as automatic, planned migration, or blocked; never forward arbitrary source SQL. Reconcile catalogs after nontransactional DDL, restarts, and uncertain responses. Existing-target paths: compatible empty tables; nonempty staging/shadow comparison/publication; explicit merge policies using reliable keys; or incremental onboarding with proven matching data and log position. Entering a GTID without a verified baseline is insufficient. Keyless merges require multiset rules, not guessed upserts. Report extra/conflicting rows and trigger/FK side effects before changing anything; no automatic clearing. Relax Gauss business secondary UNIQUE to ordinary indexes; permit capability-driven relaxation for incompatible constraints on other targets, retaining original definitions. Preserve PK/candidate identity, internal deduplication, and required analytical materialization keys. Report missing equivalents instead of inventing indexes. See index policy for GSI and constraint restoration. 7. Three journal deployment modes Mode Use Availability/recovery limits --- --- --- LOCAL Single-host/Docker without extra services; persistent directory/PVC Process recovery; cross-node takeover requires original logs, authoritative owner verification, and old-writer fencing, otherwise automatic HA is disabled TARGET Reuse a validated transactional target's metadata schema No independent store, but its outage may block capture; not the default for ClickHouse/Hive/MQ-only tasks EXTERNAL Independent HA journal/state adapter and worker takeover Better isolation, but validate backend/acknowledgment/reclamation; arbitrary shared folders/object stores are not inherently safe journals Durable acknowledgment, checksums, transaction completion, stream sequence, and ownership form one protocol. Spill large transactions to durable fragments without marking partial transactions captured. Transactional sinks must not split an atomic source transaction just to save memory. Diagnose limits or use an explicitly supported mode rather than OOM and lose recovery context. Reclaim according to the slowest active subscription and baseline dependencies. Alert/backpressure near quotas and show retention headroom. Abandoning a target's history requires an explicit resnapshot plan. A message broker as sink and as internal journal are different roles; a sink connector does not automatically implement its journal backend. 8. Seven messaging families Target Adapter concerns --- --- Kafka Partitioning, durable acknowledgments, producer idempotence/transactions, transactional-ID fencing, schema/compression; restart/external-checkpoint recovery still required Pulsar Partition/routing, stable producer identity/sequence, persistent topics, deduplication windows/transactions RabbitMQ Durable queues/messages, publisher confirms, mandatory/returns, uncertain resend after reconnect, bindings RocketMQ Versioned normal/FIFO support, routing keys, acknowledgment/retry; transactional messages do not automatically couple source-log commits ActiveMQ Classic / Artemis Separate protocol/driver profiles, persistent messages, session/send acknowledgments, transactions/reconnect; Artemis features do not imply Classic parity Redis Streams XADD, persistence/replication, streams/groups and retention; generated stream IDs do not replace eventId NATS JetStream Durable streams, publish acknowledgment, subjects/consumers, deduplication IDs/windows, quotas; not ephemeral Core NATS The common contract is at-least-once publication with stable eventId and consumer idempotency by event ID/row version. Start with JSON envelopes and allow Avro/Protobuf/schema-registry plugins without a mandatory registry. Preserve type information and notify versioned schema/DDL changes. Choose per-table/key ordering or whole-transaction single-partition routing. Partitions, redelivery, and concurrent consumers do not imply global order. Large messages/transactions require transaction IDs, fragment ordinals, completion counts/markers, and checksums; atomic consumer application waits for complete assembly. Boundary records identify filtering scope so consumers do not wait for excluded rows. Kafka/Pulsar broker transactions, deduplication windows, or idempotent producers do not automatically provide end-to-end exactly-once across source, broker, and arbitrary consumer databases. RabbitMQ explicitly documents duplicates after lost confirmations. RabbitMQ reliability. Every adapter needs uncertain-commit recovery tests. Redis Streams and JetStream have their own retention, acknowledgment, persistence, and deduplication configurations; API availability is not durable-delivery validation. Redis Streams, JetStream. Validate ActiveMQ variants separately: Classic transactions, Artemis deduplication. Never skip bad messages by default. Missing routes, oversized messages, and serialization failures pause publication with guided UI repair. Any future quarantine-and-continue mode must retain replayable events and explicitly downgrade transaction/completeness guarantees. Broker retention/consumer completion are separate monitoring layers after publication; publish progress must not claim every subscriber has processed an event. 9. Fault model Cover source promotion/replication I/O and SQL errors, split writers, process/node failure, target outages/SQL errors, uncertain commits, disk full/corruption, interrupted DDL, lost MQ acknowledgments, duplicates/reordering, partial analytical batches, upgrades, and backup rollback. Retry transient errors with backoff; pause affected subscriptions for deterministic issues. Restarts/standby activation never bypass pause. UI exposes cause, scope, last safe positions, backlog, and recommended actions, then retries the original unit after repair. Do not offer casual position editing/transaction skipping. External database HA owns promotion/old-primary isolation; CDC cannot reconstruct permanently lost source data. 10. Graphical workbench Wizard: scenario → connections/tests → objects/privileges → compatibility/constraints/storage/sizing → explicit mapping → execution plan → run/diagnose → barrier validation → cutover/handover. Pages include overview, connections/drivers, tasks/subscriptions, object differences, journal/capacity, indexes/DDL, validation, incident center, cutover plans, deployment diagnostics, and audit. Explain causes/next steps in plain language; experts can expand SQLState/vendor codes and sanitized diagnostics. Stable codes have equivalent Chinese/English explanations. Pause/resume, retry, mapping/concurrency changes, object repair, table rebuild, validation, and cutover use authorized APIs with request IDs, expected configuration versions, idempotency, background-operation state, and audit. Browsers never edit metadata tables directly. Destructive plans show affected objects/recovery points without default data deletion. CLI/files use the same service contract for automation/offline operation. Separate viewer, operator, migration, and credential roles. Never put passwords in logs/plain exports. Provide offline help, diagnostic bundles, metrics/alerts; telemetry upload is not a runtime requirement. UI recovery does not replace database administrators repairing source replication. 11. Linux, Docker, Kubernetes Linux delivery includes distributions, configuration, start/status/stop/upgrade procedures, and systemd. Docker includes pinned images, health checks, durable mounts, and credential injection. Declare x86 64/ARM64, JDK/driver, and native dependencies only after validation; Java bytecode portability does not prove native-library portability. Deliver both Helm Chart (values/schema, templates, upgrades, persistence options) and native YAML (applicable ConfigMaps, Secret references, Services, workloads, probes, RBAC, PVCs), usable with kubectl apply. Maintain both through the same configuration model and render/consistency checks. Test defaults/local volumes/external storage/HA/upgrades; screenshots or hand-written-resource instructions are insufficient. Local authoritative journals require recoverable volumes and single-writer policy; shared-journal workers may have no authoritative local state. Replica count is not safe takeover, and RWO is not fencing. Validate/version configuration/Secret changes. Graceful stop completes or rolls back the current safe unit and releases ownership. Separate liveness, readiness, and subscription status to avoid restart storms during source outages or pauses. Support private registries, offline dependencies/driver packages, and certificates. Cryptographic, OS/CPU, and vendor certifications require actual dependency/testing records; do not claim certification by default. 12. Hardware/performance standard Deliver benchmark tools, workload definitions, raw reports, and sizing guidance rather than invented rows-per-core figures. 4C/8GiB, 8C/16GiB, and 16C/32GiB may be experimental tiers , not measured throughput or production minimums. Record source, worker, journal, and each target's hardware separately. Record CPU model/architecture/quota, RAM/heap, disk type/capacity/measured bandwidth/IOPS/durability settings, network RTT/bandwidth, product/driver versions, tables/indexes, row width, JSON/LOB, identity class, transaction sizes, operation mix, target count, batches/concurrency, and acknowledgment policy. Measure snapshot rows/s and MiB/s, CDC events/s and transactions/s, end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency, visibility delay, backlog growth, takeover/catch-up time, resource use, source business impact, and final validation. Separate keyless, fan-out, MQ, JSON, and transaction-size cases. Narrow single-table benchmarks cannot represent all deployments. For backlog B, incoming rate r, and apply capacity c in matching units, sustained catch-up requires c r; ideal catch-up time is B/(c-r). Journal sizing approximates durable log rate × required retention plus active snapshot artifacts, large-transaction staging, index/metadata space, and margin, adjusted for measured compression/write amplification. More hardware cannot remove hot-key ordering, source/target bottlenecks, or network limits. 13. Migration, parallel service, extensions Scenario Boundary and extension --- --- Online migration/read-only mirrors Snapshot+CDC, data/object reconciliation, secondary-constraint conversion, migration reports Both environments serving reads One authoritative writer; route reads according to table/target watermarks and explicit staleness budget Gradual/domain cutover Explicit table/domain ownership, application routing, cross-domain transaction boundaries; service does not silently change application endpoints Independent writers to the same table Requires bidirectional capture, conflict rules, origin/loop prevention, key allocation, repair; two opposing tasks are insufficient Failback after cutover Before new business writes, planned routing rollback may suffice; afterwards require verified reverse capture/compensation and validation Real-time warehouse/events ClickHouse/Doris/Hive and all seven messaging families with traceable events/schemas Application compatibility SQL/object assessment, read-only shadow queries, interface regression, performance reports; data migration does not automatically port application SQL Cutover gates include freezing relevant source writes/DDL, final barriers, target apply/visibility, data validation, restored constraints/generated behavior, synchronization fencing, and application handover. Open new writes only after required gates pass; do not promise automatic application changes or unconditional zero downtime. Extensions include lineage/audit, history/CDC archiving, data-quality rules, masked distribution, rehearsals, and capacity forecasts. Transformations/masking mark outputs as transformed, not exact mirrors. PostgreSQL/Oracle capture should be later connector milestones before corresponding reverse paths can be validated. Active-active conflict merging and cross-environment global transactions are separate advanced projects, not implied first-release guarantees. 14. Delivery sequence and completion Phase Delivery/acceptance --- --- P0 Foundation Rename, source-neutral events/positions/SPI, capability matrix, configuration versions, task/subscription isolation; preserve existing recovery regressions P1 Correctness/UI foundation Keyless/JSON/generated columns, baseline/DDL recovery, relational targets, wizard/incidents; object/transaction/fault matrix P2 Storage/distribution Three journals, fan-out, all in-scope MQ, ClickHouse/Doris/Hive; lost ACK/duplicates/reordering/partial batches/quotas P3 Migration closure Existing targets, validation/repair, constraint restoration, cutover gates/audit, Linux/Docker/Helm/native YAML, full bilingual manual P4 Performance/product acceptance Hardware benchmarks, soak/fault/upgrade matrix, security configuration/offline delivery; truthful status per target Later source milestones PostgreSQL/Oracle connectors and snapshot/long-transaction/failover acceptance before verified reverse paths Phasing does not demote in-scope message targets or objects to optional suggestions. Every stage delivers runnable functionality, matching UI, bilingual documentation, and fault tests. Do not mark design-only adapters available. Apache preparation separately includes name review, community/governance, ownership/dependency terms, LICENSE/NOTICE, reproducible builds, and test infrastructure. Rivomesh is not currently an Apache project. ASF naming.

title: Reconciliation workflow
text: Data reconciliation, repair and a common cut The common barrier, MySQL consistent view, private disk staging, transactional SQL row comparison and CLI are implemented. The LOCAL/H2 and external PostgreSQL/MySQL/openGauss barrier profiles passed native acceptance; the newer row-comparison scope is recorded separately. The first COMMON CUT repair CLI is now accepted in the linked repair handbook; the first managed repair UI is separately accepted;other compensation modes and cutover remain incomplete. Implemented foundation SourceAdapter.ConsistentRead represents one view across tables. Source-specific covers interprets position coverage; generic SourcePosition does not order GTID/LSN/SCN strings. MySQL uses GTID-set coverage. PipelineValidationBarrier.open(config, selectedTargets, maximumGateMillis, maximumReadMillis) checks the existing journal identity/running state/completed snapshots, obtains a bounded MySQL global read lock, establishes one REPEATABLE READ view and pins declared table metadata across configured databases. It records the source cut, waits for capture/normalization and selected target ACKs, then rechecks generation/epoch/position/sequence/snapshot acknowledgments under the journal job lock before persistently pausing and incrementing the epoch. Selected SQL targets acquire local transactional fences and must report the same sequence. JdbcSink.existing never creates lost checkpoint metadata. The source write gate is released while its MVCC view remains available for table reads. Unselected targets can be paused or offline; they are not presented as validated. The certificate contains source/capture positions, configuration fingerprint, generation, epoch, sequence, error version, schema hashes and selected target checkpoints. It proves a synchronization boundary, not row equality. Concurrent control or checkpoint changes invalidate eligibility. Source writes may continue after gate release; the task stays paused until explicit recovery processes later binlog events. Bounds and recovery The explicit source-gate limit is1–120seconds; the read session has a separate limit, at least as long and at most24hours. Deadlines abort owned connections, with session wait timeout as an additional cleanup measure. No global settings are changed. Network failures prevent an exact millisecond guarantee of server-side unlock; monitor database sessions as well. The source MVCC transaction holds table metadata locks and old row versions, which can delay DDL and grow undo. Native tests observe actual lock waits and release. Early closure of an unfinished cursor aborts the entire validation view instead of draining an unbounded result or treating a partial scan as complete. SIGKILL releases connections; durable pause cannot be bypassed by restart. Lost MVCC views cannot be reconstructed from files; incomplete source scans need a new cut. Fence failure retains the persisted pause. The protocol assumes a consistent writable destination endpoint and does not replace database HA routing/old-primary isolation. Selected destinations currently use transactional SQL. MQ producer acknowledgement is not downstream data validation; analytical visibility/materialization requires product-specific support. Primary MySQL references: consistent snapshots, FLUSH, session timeouts. Row comparison and CLI The synchronizer must be the only writer of destination business tables. Begin with a RUNNING pipeline, completed snapshots and selected targets able to reach the common cut. Establishing the cut briefly blocks writes across the MySQL instance. After releasing source writes, the pipeline stays PAUSED until explicitly resumed. CLI defaults:30second source gate,1hour source view,10minutes per destination table,1GiB logical staging budget and4MiB per row. Java callers can set explicit limits. Source rows, target rows and keyless identity records all consume the budget; it is not a1GiB source-data allowance. Physical-file checks run at batch commit boundaries; H2 pages/indexes/temporary data can require additional space. Use filesystem/container quotas for a hard physical limit. Large-scale capacity remains unaccepted. The source scan uses the original MVCC view. Keyless occurrence IDs are paged from the durable journal and matched against the complete canonical source multiset. Only complete source scans are sealed. Supported POSIX systems use0700directories/0600files, with same-process and cross-process writer locks. Staging is not encrypted; place it on appropriately private storage. Each destination scan holds the physical checkpoint row lock on the same connection used for reading. Ownership, schema, completed snapshot and exact checkpoint are checked without recreating metadata, advancing sequence or modifying business rows. Types share the synchronization canonicalization contract. Keyless internal identities are compared as well as values; equal data with wrong identities yields missing and extra differences. MySQL TIME expressions are explicitly cast to CHAR for source snapshots, consistent views, virtual-generated evaluation and target validation. This avoids JDBC temporal formatting losing a negative subsecond sign: -00:00:00.000001 must remain negative one microsecond. MySQL FLOAT32 targets explicitly use FLOAT; default-mode REAL aliases DOUBLE, as documented in the official numeric type reference. Existing incorrect table types need an explicit migration plan; validation never alters them automatically. Per-target/table results contain counts, content roots and missing , extra , changed totals. Equal results produce VALIDATION MATCH , otherwise VALIDATION DIFFERENCES . The Java store supports identity-hash keyset pages of up to200differences. Summaries omit business row values; raw values in private staging remain sensitive. Recovery boundaries: - An interrupted incomplete source scan cannot resume its lost MVCC cursor. Inspect the durable pause, explicitly resume as appropriate and establish a new cut. Never mix source views. - Once source data is sealed, validate-compare checks configuration/generation/epoch/error version/positions and physical target checkpoints, validates the source seal and row checksums, discards partial destination scans and rereads them. The source database need not be online during this phase. - Resuming/reconfiguring the pipeline or changing checkpoints invalidates continued comparison. Historical reports remain readable and do not prove current equality. - Success, failure and timeout all retain the pause. Use the current error version with the existing status / resume-pipeline controls to resume explicitly. The first end-to-end native comparison profile uses MySQL8.4 sources and PostgreSQL17/MySQL8.4 destinations. Other transactional adapters share the reader interface but their vendor/version/mode/distributed acceptance remains separate. Messaging and analytical destinations do not yet implement this comparison protocol. FAQ - Why did replication stop advancing after validation? Establishing the cut durably pauses it. Review the report/task state and explicitly resume using the current error version. Monitor source binlog retention and journal capacity while paused. - Can a longer timeout resume an incomplete source scan? A lost MySQL MVCC transaction cannot be reconstructed. Keep the failed report, follow explicit task recovery and establish a new cut with an appropriate read budget. - Why can equal keyless business values still produce missing/extra rows? Incorrect occurrence IDs break later UPDATE/DELETE processing. Counts or business-value-only comparison would miss this. - Can I rewrite hashes after VALIDATION SOURCE SEAL MISMATCH ? Do not alter the summary/H2 contents to force acceptance. It can indicate corruption, changed data or a development-era report format difference. Retain evidence and establish a new validation run; historical summaries remain useful for diagnosis. - Did validation repair rows or rebuild UNIQUE constraints? No. It only reads destinations. Reviewed repair and pre-takeover constraint restoration require subsequent workflows. Remaining workflow The first management jobs, cancellation, summaries, task grants and report audit now have bilingual UI/API. ADMIN raw difference-row details are now implemented; complete report catalogs/retention, richer retry/quota planning and job/controller HA remain pending. Keyless repair must retain journal occurrence IDs. Additional vendor/type/mode/fault profiles remain to be verified. Reviewed repair plans must show affected objects/counts/boundaries, enforce authorization/configuration versions/idempotency/audit, commit business repair and native receipts locally without rewriting the synchronization GTID/sequence, and resolve lost responses. Arbitrary nonempty adoption and failed-transaction compensation/skip need separate consistency-gap handling. Final cutover needs a fresh final source barrier, target visibility/data checks, restored constraints and write handoff; an earlier historical cut after source writes resumed is not a current takeover permit. 中文 The first managed workflow now supports destination selection, background jobs, cancellation, target retries and table summaries. See Managed validation. ADMIN raw difference-row UI is now implemented. Managed repair UI is now separately accepted;cutover UI remains pending. The first COMMON CUT repair CLI now has four-journal native acceptance for MySQL/PostgreSQL. It is separate from validation-only operations and has a separately accepted authenticated managed workflow;see transaction compensation for the separate SQL workflow. Business cutover remains open.

title: Recovery & consistency
text: V2 recovery, primary failover and consistency 中文：恢复、主库切换与一致性. This document describes the v2 single-database, single-target core . V3 uses MVCC snapshot artifacts, a separate journal and independent destinations: follow the V3 manual and message contract. V2 state cannot be adopted simply by setting formatVersion: 3 . Service ownership Processes create v2 metadata idempotently, handling concurrent catalog creation separately. Initial task configuration and discovered-table manifests are inserted atomically. Conditional updates claim the owner and lease; a separate heartbeat renews the lease, and data/progress transactions check the same owner. Each new work session uses a new owner identity so callbacks from an older replication connection cannot commit into the new session. The task-row lock serializes capture, snapshot and application commits. After ownership transfers, the old owner is rejected before business writes and cannot pause or release the new owner's task. Standby nodes do not open binlog connections; a healthy task normally has one replication client. Persistent GTID state - capture gtid : the initial baseline plus committed source transactions durably queued or irrelevant to the selected business database. - required gtid : the union of captured transactions and the GTIDs required by source state already read during snapshot/discovery. - applied sequence : the queued transaction sequence already applied to business tables. Physical UUIDs and file positions support diagnostics and backend validation; cross-server recovery uses GTIDs. A complete source commit is persisted before adding its GTID to capture gtid . The connector's possibly earlier in-memory GTID is never copied directly over persistent progress. Duplicate GTIDs are checked under the task lock and do not enqueue the same durable transaction twice. Primary failover during a snapshot After recording baseline B0, capture FULL row images while scanning by primary-key cursor. Every chunk records a source GTID watermark after reading; its business rows, last key and read dependency commit together. Discovery and initial scan-upper-bound reads also contribute to required gtid . A snapshot may have read a transaction from the former primary before the capture connection persisted it. Validating only capture gtid would miss that dependency. A failover candidate must therefore include required gtid . After all chunks complete, record B1, wait until capture gtid includes B1, then replay the queue in source commit order. The scan imports unchanged rows; the final full row image or DELETE establishes the result for changed rows. Primary-key changes remove the old key and write the new key. Logs cover inserts before the scan cursor and beyond the initial upper bound. During snapshot and early replay, the target is not a consistent image of one source instant. During continuous incremental application, every source transaction, including cross-table changes, is applied in one destination transaction. This v2 cursor approach differs from v3's restart/rebase of an incomplete MVCC snapshot. Primary discovery and selection 1. Probe candidate addresses for UUID, server id, read-only state, GTID mode, executed/purged sets and replication health. 2. In ordinary primary/replica topologies, select only a writable node without active upstream threads or residual replication errors. 3. For Group Replication, require ONLINE, PRIMARY, writable and single-primary mode. 4. Multiple writable primaries require external isolation; the service does not arbitrarily choose one. 5. Require required gtid ⊆ candidate.gtid executed ; otherwise wait for catch-up. 6. Require candidate.gtid purged ⊆ capture gtid ; otherwise necessary uncaptured history may already be unavailable, so block progress. 7. Reconnect with persistent GTID auto-positioning. Automatic fallback to the purged set is disabled. JDBC queries validate physical UUID and writability; the replication connection validates its handshake server id before processing events. If a router/VIP sends these connections to different backends, abandon the session and rediscover. Heartbeat expiry, disconnection or source role changes also establish a new session from persistent GTIDs. Operators must ensure candidates belong to the same logical topology, replicate all selected data, and have no filtering or forged GTIDs. Equal GTID sets cannot detect every manual data modification. CDC cannot reconstruct permanently lost asynchronous transactions that never reached a surviving candidate. Rivomesh does not promote MySQL nodes. Transaction boundaries Operation Contents committed in one destination transaction --- --- Create task Configuration fingerprint, B0, table manifest, scan upper bounds and discovery watermark Snapshot chunk Business rows, cursor, row count, completion state and read-dependency GTIDs Capture commit Complete ordered row events, origin, GTID, capture/required sets Apply commit All row changes, applied sequence, phase changes and queue deletion Record failure Error history, shared run state, safe context and owner release An uncertain commit ends the current work session. The new session rereads persistent progress instead of reusing an old in-memory cursor/GTID. Business tables, queues and state tables must be backed up/restored as one recovery unit. SQL errors and shared pause Connection/serialization SQL states 08/40, lock waits and recoverable resource failures retry with backoff. Data, constraints, permissions and syntax errors pause. Safe error context includes table, source GTID, queued transaction sequence, SQLState and vendor code; row payloads and SQL literals are excluded. A failed destination transaction rolls back completely and retains the queue head. Capture may already have safely persisted later commits; application does not pass the failed transaction. PAUSED is shared database state: restarting or adding standby processes cannot bypass it. Repair the cause, then resume the original transaction. Resume does not skip rows, alter GTIDs or empty queues. Database operators repair source replication SQL errors. The service does not execute SQL SLAVE SKIP COUNTER, inject empty GTIDs or RESET. A failed replica does not interrupt capture from a healthy primary; promotion of that unhealthy replica is rejected until repaired and caught up. V1 file-position tasks lack complete GTIDs and read dependencies. Automatic in-place upgrade is refused and old state is preserved. Consult validation for accepted versions and fault profiles; current-format transactional SQL targets have separate reviewed recovery profiles. Configuration-format migration and automated business cutover remain open.

title: Rename migration
text: Rivomesh rename and existing-task migration Updated: 2026-11-17. 中文：更名迁移. The Java base package and Maven groupId are now io.github.rivomesh . Entry points, reflective loading, relocated drivers, tests and deployment scripts use that namespace. Rebuild every module; do not reuse transport SDK JARs or compiled directories from the previous namespace. The initial public repository is <https://github.com/rivomesh/rivomesh . Historical scripts, source manifests, logs and checksums under docs/verification/ retain their original package names and belong to their historical candidates. They do not certify the renamed build. See implementation status for current recovery evidence and outstanding compatibility profiles. This change migrates project identity/build references without changing replication algorithms, v2 state formats, configuration fingerprints, or SQL-error handling. Names Object New value --- --- Project / root Maven artifactId Rivomesh / rivomesh Directory rivomesh , alongside canal Maven groupId / Java base package io.github.rivomesh Executable artifactId / entry point rivomesh-app / io.github.rivomesh.Main Relocated driver artifactId / JDBC class rivomesh-gaussdb-driver / io.github.rivomesh.gaussdb.jdbc.Driver Source module directories Retain sync-app and gaussdb-driver ; directory names need not equal artifactIds Technical naming does not establish domain/trademark ownership or Apache acceptance; review separately before public release. Existing installations 1. Stop every old service node for the task; do not mix driver-package versions on one task. 2. Back up configuration and business/management data as one recovery unit. Preserve jobId, logical clusterId, source database, target URL/schema, and metadata schema. Never delete state or clear business tables for a rename. 3. Change any explicit target driver to io.github.rivomesh.gaussdb.jdbc.Driver ; omitting it selects the new default. Do not substitute the test PostgreSQL driver for the relocated Gauss driver. 4. Update working directories, classpaths, JAR paths, monitoring/log references to sync-app/target/rivomesh-app-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar . Recompile custom code using renamed entry/model classes. 5. Run check/status, verify existing state, then run. PAUSED remains paused; repair and resume rather than bypassing errors through renaming. Moving the root does not update external file contents. Check relative paths against the new working directory. Private local.yml is not rewritten automatically; repository examples/defaults are updated. Recovery boundary The rename introduces no multi-source/multi-target/new-journal state format. Those changes require separate migrations, compatibility checks, and rollback plans; package changes alone cannot make incompatible checkpoints reusable. See README and validation for current operation, and platform design for planned capabilities.

title: Requirements & decisions
text: Rivomesh requirements, decisions, and implementation boundaries Updated: 2026-11-16. 中文：需求与决策. This document records scope and implementation status. Accepted requirements are not released features. See the README for current operation and platform design for capabilities and scenarios. New/clarified scope and gaps use SDD baseline RM-SDD-001:48traceable requirements,tasks and acceptance contracts. Current behavior remains governed by implementation status and evidence. Confirmed decisions ID Decision Current implementation --- --- --- D01 Each independent task configuration binds one logical source, initially MySQL; the platform may manage multiple configurations/independent sources, with standalone task deployment retained Web/CLI support v2/v3, multi-database/target wizard, independent recovery and journal selection D02 Select multiple databases per topology with explicit target instance/database/schema mappings Web/CLI v3 implement databases and per-target mappings ; see V3 manual D03 Fan out one source to multiple targets/products Web/CLI v3 implement independent target ACKs, fault isolation and recovery D04 Support MySQL5.7/8.0/8.2/8.4 sources;accept standalone/GTID ASYNC/single-primary MGR per profile Basic5.7,historical8.0 V2/HA and representative8.4 V3 evidence exist;8.2 dedicated acceptance and the full matrix remain D05 Broad MySQL,PostgreSQL,openGauss,distributed GaussDB,DM,Kingbase,OceanBase and GBase product/version/mode scope Specified initial MySQL/PG/openGauss/DM/Kingbase/GBase8c profiles exist;distributed GaussDB,full OceanBase recovery,GBase8a/8s and more modes remain D06 Relax Gauss business secondary UNIQUE to ordinary indexes, avoiding GSI solely for those indexes; permit relaxation for compatibility issues on other targets V3 ordinary secondary indexes/business UNIQUE downgrade implemented; GSI has model plans; distributed hardware acceptance pending D07 Only the synchronization service writes subscribed target tables; validate and restore required constraints before takeover Exclusive writes currently required; takeover workflow planned D08 Automatic recovery does not skip;manual skip/compensation requires review,original evidence and gaps;database promotion stays external Some ASYNC/MGR/worker takeover and original-transaction retry pass;reviewed skip and compensation have bounded SQL acceptance D09 Linux manual, Docker, Kubernetes Helm Chart and native manifests, comprehensive bilingual manuals/FAQ Deployment files and bilingual operations manual provided; live K8s/full-platform acceptance remain D10 Final name Rivomesh, directory rivomesh , Java package/Maven groupId io.github.rivomesh Renamed in this change; no claim of domain/trademark clearance or Apache status D11 Include no-PK tables, JSON, and STORED/VIRTUAL generated columns in first-release scope V3 keyless multisets, JSON, STORED and whitelisted VIRTUAL materialization implemented/tested D12 Optional independent log storage; deployment with or without it V3 H2 local and PostgreSQL/openGauss/MySQL external journals with independent ACKs/safe reclamation implemented D13 Broad support for existing nonempty targets, object differences, and takeover Initial targets must be empty;COMMON CUT repair exists while nonempty adoption/merge remains pending D14 Publish reproducible hardware/workload/performance standards instead of universal TPS promises Benchmark tooling and small SQL/JDK smoke evidence exist;representative capacity standards and soak remain D15 Complete bilingual UI,wizards,diagnostics and guided recovery Local workbench,grants,configuration,validation and MySQL/PG COMMON CUT repair exist;shared sessions, fixed-owner controls and reviewed SQL recovery have scoped profiles. Cutover remains open D16 Government/enterprise domestic-database migration, staged switching, and parallel environments One-way mirroring is the foundation; ownership/takeover/failback boundaries in platform design D17 ClickHouse,Apache Doris,Apache Hive and extensible analytical destinations All three have initial materialization/recovery profiles;cluster/security/capacity/all-JDK gates remain without relational-transaction promises D18 Kafka,Pulsar,RabbitMQ,RocketMQ,ActiveMQ Classic/Artemis,Redis Streams and NATS JetStream All have initial transport/recovery evidence;complete cluster/TLS/capacity and new skip/compensation protocols need per-adapter acceptance D19 PostgreSQL and Oracle sources are committed implementation scope,with neutral SPI/events/positions retained Actual sources remain MySQL;PG/Oracle SOURCE is PLANNED and native snapshot/CDC/recovery remains D20 Unified multi-node inventory/control;any entry manages remote tasks Worker lease/owner foundations exist;global registry,remote command plane and control HA do not D21 Login survives reload with logout,expiry,revocation and cross-controller policy Current token is page-memory-only;server sessions/reload restoration remain D22 Reviewed transaction skip,controlled source-gap recovery and guided manual corrective data Bounded SQL profiles have reviewed transaction skip, gap verification and manual corrections D23 Java8/11/17/21/25 require real current-release profile evidence Java8 baseline and an older ten-profile SQL matrix exist;complete current-platform/driver/recovery matrix remains D24 Use SDD specification/design/task/acceptance tracing and complete bilingual docs RM-SDD-001 v0.2 closes4single-controller session requirements;44remain tracked The platform boundary is one source per task, multiple tasks per platform . No implicit source merging or cross-source transactions. Isolated workers may run under one console or as separate deployments. source.nodes still lists candidates in one topology. Isolate task IDs, state namespaces, quotas, and replication client server IDs; reject overlapping target tables by default. Multiple databases and targets This example expresses product intent. For runnable configuration see the V3 manual and config/pipeline-v3.yml : Task MySQL database Target instance Target namespace --- --- --- --- sales orders gauss-a app / orders sales crm gauss-a app / crm sales orders doris-b analytics / orders legacy finance dm-c Explicit product-specific namespace Version mappings and check case rules, reserved words, shortened names, and collisions. New subscriptions establish their own baseline rather than reusing another cursor. Independent configurations capture separately by default; sharing requires explicit association and compatible source identity, filters, security, and storage policies. Within a v3 task, the runner shares ordered logs and routes events with independent snapshot, delivery/application/visibility positions and errors per target. One target's SQL failure should not pause others; shared decoding failures may affect all targets in that task. Apply complete source transactions atomically where the relational target supports that scope. No cross-target XA is introduced. Probe Doris single/multi-table transaction support per version; use dedicated batch/materialization protocols for ClickHouse/Hive. Reject unmet task consistency requirements, or require an explicit weaker mode explained by the UI. Recovery and log storage Preserve atomic data/local-checkpoint commits and owner fencing for transactional sinks. Other sinks require replayable batches, resolved commit acknowledgments, deduplication/versioning, and visibility watermarks. Advancing an external checkpoint first is not a substitute. Mode No extra independent store Failure boundary --- --- --- Local durable journal Yes; persistent directory/volume Process recovery; permanent disk loss is not guaranteed lossless; cross-node takeover requires original logs and reliable fencing Target-hosted journal Yes, for targets with required transactional/state capabilities Failure of that target can block capture; arbitrary analytics engines cannot host the current Gauss metadata unchanged Independent shared journal No; an explicitly supported HA backend Enables cross-node worker recovery, subject to journal availability/capacity Persist logs before capture GTID advances. Reclaim only after all active subscriptions and baseline dependencies permit it. Alert/backpressure at quotas rather than silently discard unconsumed data. Per-task quotas must prevent one offline target from exhausting the platform. Failover verifies captured and all relevant snapshot-read dependency GTIDs. CDC cannot recover permanently lost source transactions; editing GTIDs must not bypass gaps. Distributed metadata needs compatible keys/constraints and a durable stream sequence, not CN-generated IDs, timestamps, or lexical GTID ordering. Compatibility and index policy Broad support means capability detection and a matrix identifying product/version/mode/engine/driver, objects, and consistency level. Distinguish verified, experimental, unverified, and unsupported. JDBC connectivity does not prove replication support; a feature in one release cannot be assumed for older versions. Other targets may relax incompatible business secondary UNIQUE constraints into ordinary indexes or supported access structures, with an explicit difference manifest. Report the absence of an equivalent structure honestly. Candidate identity keys on no-PK tables, technical keys, and Doris/ClickHouse materialization keys are not optional business secondary constraints. See Gauss index policy and platform design. Decisions no longer blocking design Broad product coverage, hardware-based performance standards, optional storage, no-PK/JSON/generated columns, existing targets, conditional UNIQUE relaxation, Rivomesh naming, independent configurations, and Web UI are confirmed. Do not repeatedly ask whether these features are needed. An onboarding wizard obtains actual versions, modes, namespaces, volumes, and privileges and produces compatibility/sizing reports. Listing every future customer environment now is unnecessary. Conflict priorities for existing data, destructive changes, and production switching still require task-specific choices; broad compatibility does not authorize arbitrary overwrites/deletions. Classify DDL by operation/capability: additions, compatible changes, destructive changes, generated-expression changes, and partition changes, with automatic, planned-migration, or blocked outcomes. Including the three requested object types does not imply every MySQL engine/function/DDL is automatically compatible. Delivery and acceptance Suggested order: rename → capability/task isolation → identity/JSON/generated columns/DDL → optional journals/adapters → UI recovery/validation → takeover → full benchmark/delivery matrix. Deliver UI operations alongside core features rather than waiting for every adapter. Test task isolation, cross-database transactions, target-specific recovery, journal GC/backpressure, duplicate counts on keyless tables, historical generated expressions, JSON precision, existing-target reconciliation, analytics retry/visibility, source failover, and stale owners. Validation separately records v2 HA, v3 three-target/two-journal, HTTP/DOM and broker tests. Repeated executions are not summed as distinct cases; remaining scope needs dedicated acceptance. FAQ Can configurations connect to independent MySQL sources? Yes. The platform now loads independent configurations and manages isolated workers/checkpoints. Standalone CLI remains. See console manual for boundaries. Do parallel environments imply writes to the same table on both sides? No. Start with one writer/multiple readers, shadow validation, or explicit domain ownership. Independent writers require additional source capture, conflict resolution, loop prevention, and application routing beyond current one-way MySQL CDC. Can every target share identical DDL/write SQL? No. Reuse the event model; adapters own types, indexes, transactions, batch commits, and reading semantics. Are all new features available now? No. Renaming, v3 fan-out, keyless/JSON/supported generated columns, optional journals, Web and Kafka/RabbitMQ/NATS/Redis Streams/Pulsar/RocketMQ are implemented. Complete DDL, remaining adapters, permissions/repair and business switching remain in development. Enable features according to the implementation/validation matrices.

title: Security audit
text: Security audit, retention and export 中文：安全审计. This records management API/controller events separately from the 40-operation task history and configuration revisions. Scope and permissions Only ADMIN can read/export or open Security audit . VIEWER/OPERATOR attempts are denied and audited. API requests record HTTP BEGIN / HTTP END : authenticated actor/role, fixed route category, known task ID, direct peer IP, HTTP status and safe error code. Authentication failures have no actor and status 401; authorization/Origin denials record 403. Health probes/static files are excluded. Raw URLs/queries, Authorization, bodies, credentials, rows and exception text are excluded. Client request IDs are SHA-256 hashes for correlation, not raw arbitrary headers. Forwarded IP headers are not trusted. HTTP END means response prepared, not delivered. A 202 is not successful execution. OPERATION COMMITTED records durable PENDING and SUCCEEDED/FAILED outcomes, actor and operation-request hash; configuration edit/restore outcomes are included. Startup/orderly shutdown have separate events. Internal calls without HTTP attribution and older history are not assigned invented identities. CLI replication, business SQL and OS activity are outside this controller audit. Durability and failures dataDirectory/audit/events.mv.db uses H2 transactions, synchronous writes, contiguous sequences and a SHA-256 chain. The private audit directory is 0700 and database 0600 where POSIX permissions exist; protect other platforms with ACLs. Startup verifies the retained chain/tail. The controller registry binds the audit store identity: deleting/replacing it with a new empty database refuses startup. Stop the controller and coherently back up registry, audit, configuration revisions and journals; copying a live H2 file is not a consistent backup. An API begin event must persist before the request executes. Failure returns 503 AUDIT UNAVAILABLE , preventing that HTTP management action. Already accepted asynchronous results commit an outbox entry with controller state, then append the event. A crash between append and outbox removal replays by event ID without duplication. If completion was committed but audit/outbox cleanup failed, the operation may have happened: inspect/replay its original request ID and revision, rather than blindly submitting a new request. A BEGIN without an END means the result needs investigation. Audit failures do not terminate independent replication workers. Management requests are blocked while process probes can remain healthy. Repair private volume capacity/permissions; restore coherent backups for chain corruption or identity mismatch. Never erase audit files to bypass verification. Retention auditMaxEvents defaults to 1000000, range 1000–10000000. Set it in Linux/Docker platform YAML, Helm --set platform.auditMaxEvents=2000000 , or the native ConfigMap, followed by a controlled restart. The UI/API expose the limit and pruning anchor. Each new-event transaction prunes the old prefix while retaining anchorSequence/anchorHash ; the remaining history never pretends to start at zero. This count is not a physical disk byte quota: monitor H2/backup storage. Status polling also generates events; choose retention from measured request volume. Pages use fixed after/through bounds, oldest first, 100 by default, maximum 1000. after=0 selects the current retained beginning; through=0 fixes the current head. Continue with next and the same through . A cursor overtaken by retention receives 409 AUDIT HISTORY EXPIRED , never silent data omission; invalid rollback/range changes receive409 AUDIT HISTORY CHANGED . Console and exports ADMIN opens Security audit , reviews sequence/time/identity/route/task/result and uses Next page . Refresh retained window starts a new window. Export this page downloads only the current 100 events and proofs, not all history; changed boundaries prevent download. Close/sign-out clears records and fences late responses. For a full streaming export, use a management machine with Python 3 and an environment-supplied ADMIN token: The full exporter fixes one tail, verifies sequence/chain/store identity/tail hash page by page, streams to a 0600 file, writes COMPLETE, then publishes the final filename. Memory is bounded by page size. Existing outputs are never overwritten and HTTP redirects are refused. Failures/expired retention leave .partial , without a successful final file; export to a new path. Events generated during export lie beyond its fixed tail. Successful single-page verification with non-null continuation proves that page, not full-history completeness. API - GET /api/audit?after=0&through=0&limit=100 : ADMIN pages, events/next/storeId and integrity boundaries. - GET /api/audit/export?... : same range/permissions with JSON attachment headers; the streaming tool continues through this endpoint. Only those three nonnegative integer query parameters are accepted; limit is 1–1000. Reads/exports themselves are audited. Security and acceptance boundaries The local chain/registry detects ordinary corruption, missing rows and new empty-store replacement. It cannot resist an administrator rewriting all files/recomputing the chain or coherently rolling back every backup. External immutable/signature anchors, cross-controller aggregation, account management and its audit remain required work; exact task grants are documented in the authorization handbook. Keep exported tails/hashes in independent controlled custody. This is not an external immutable compliance audit service. See validation for tested profiles. Local account changes record ACCOUNT COMMITTED with subjectId and directory version; the UI shows the affected task/account. Directory mutation and audit outbox are saved together, with a separate durable version anchor unaffected by event retention. Legacy export payload/hash bytes are preserved; see accounts. External immutable anchoring remains pending.

title: Shared access
text: Shared accounts, sessions and audit 中文：共享身份. Contract. Acceptance follows implementation status and candidate evidence. Set cluster.sharedAccess: true consistently before first deployment,following thefirst-release baseline. Shared identity uses one SQL authority;restart recovery remains supported. Existing namespace modes are not automatically migrated. Global tasks additionally require sharedTasks. Bootstrap imports the selected node's verified managed directory or seeds from configured accounts. Existing shared grants are never overwritten by stale deployment tokens. Start the chosen import node first when migrating existing managed identities. Imported non-administrator accounts are restricted to the importing node to preserve their prior local access. The account editor exposes “All nodes” and selected node IDs; an empty selection grants no node access. Administrators can explicitly expand access after reviewing task-ID collisions. API nodeIds: null means all nodes, an array limits nodes, and an omitted field on update preserves the prior grant. Administrator accounts always cover all nodes. Conflicting independent managed directories are not automatically merged; review/export identities and grants before planning adoption. Back up coordinated local control/accounts/audit/configuration/reports and SQL metadata before migration. Local controller state becomes format3 and binds clusterId/shared-store identity. Old software, disabling sharedAccess and missing/wrong authority refuse startup rather than restoring stale local grants. This is the control-state format, not task formatVersion. Rollback requires coordinated backups and review of revoked credentials, not merely an old JAR. Pre-import local audit history retains its original chain/payload. The shared chain records its storeId/last-sequence/hash anchor. New HTTP/account/task-outbox events enter the shared chain; endpoints see the same storeId. pendingOperations currently counts only the responding endpoint local outbox; other nodes pending diagnostics remain future work. Local outboxes drain only after shared confirmation; duplicate IDs are idempotent and payload collisions are rejected. A login at A resumes at B and survives A shutdown/kill/restart. Logout revokes its session globally. Any directory mutation atomically updates revision, revokes all old sessions and writes account audit. Audit failure rolls the transaction back. Every authentication/grant check reads the SQL identity/policy/content marker and audit anchor; matching immutable verified payloads may be reused without offline authentication fallback; outages return503 without local/memory fallback. Session creation checks current revision and expiry uses database time. Bearer and HTTPS/Origin/CSRF rules remain in browser sessions. Members must agree on enabled/Secure/remember policy, idle/absolute expiry, session capacity and audit retention. publicOrigin can differ by direct endpoint; a common HTTPS frontend uses the same external origin. Limits:200accounts,10000task grants per account and4MiB serialized directory. Capacity rejects a change without changing prior state. Sessions share one global maximum. Audit uses auditMaxEvents; non-HTTP idempotency receipts are retained separately without automatic cleanup yet, so monitor disk growth. Retention governance remains LG-09. Worker JVMs receive essential OS variables and explicitly referenced task variables. Unreferenced parent variables/JAVA TOOL OPTIONS and management/control-store credential variables are withheld; referencing protected names returns WORKER ENVIRONMENT DENIED. Use task-specific source/target/journal settings and explicit approved TLS/Kerberos driver configuration. Workers remain trusted SDK processes under the installation user; filesystem isolation, dedicated containers/Vault and finer task-secret distribution remain CP-05 work. Deployment: enable the field in platform-cluster.yml, keeping independent local directories. Helm has values-shared-access.yaml; native YAML has shared-a / shared-b. Supply dedicated store credentials through Secret. Live Kubernetes/CSI/controller HA remain separate acceptance. Recovery and FAQ - Lost all admin tokens: stop one local controller and use the existing access-recover command with a protected configured ADMIN seed. Shared mode updates SQL authority, revokes sessions and audits recovery atomically. Verify and rotate temporary credentials. - SHARED ACCESS QUIESCENCE REQUIRED: stop all old members gracefully; STALE is not confirmed stopped. If isolation is uncertain, plan/verify it before switching, without editing STOPPED records directly. - SHARED ACCESS REQUIRED: restore the bound cluster/sharedAccess configuration; disabling it cannot revive old local tokens. - SHARED ACCESS STATE REQUIRED/IDENTITY CHANGED: restore matching SQL identity/backup/connection settings. Missing authority is never reseeded from stale configuration; do not delete local bindings. - SHARED ACCESS DIRECTORY CONFLICT: back up/export/review the independent directories before adoption/merge; privileges are not silently expanded. - SHARED ACCESS POLICY MISMATCH: align expiry/cookie/capacity/audit settings across members. - ACCOUNT DIRECTORY CAPACITY: review account/grant volume; rejected changes preserve prior state. - Recovery still shows login: check real expiry/logout/directory revocation. Valid shared sessions recover without the failed controller's memory. - Different local/shared audit sequence: they are separate store chains linked by migration anchors/event IDs. Never rewrite/concatenate historical payloads as one chain. - Can old backups restore revoked access: a consistent old backup can contain old grants. External immutable rollback detection remains unfinished; review revocation/rotation after restore.

title: Task authorization
text: Per-task authorization 中文：按任务授权. Complete example: platform-task-scopes.yml. Roles determine actions. users[].taskIds limits the tasks visible/operable by VIEWER and OPERATOR. IDs match exactly: no wildcard, prefix, database or destination-schema matching. Grants may name tasks not loaded yet. - Omitted taskIds , including older configurations, preserves deployment-wide task access, including future tasks. An explicit empty list grants no tasks. Supply the list when access must be restricted. - VIEWER reads; OPERATOR checks/starts/stops/pauses/resumes granted tasks. Neither can create/import, read/edit configuration or read global audit. - ADMIN is deployment-wide and cannot configure taskIds ; global management endpoints are not task-scoped. Keep at least one ADMIN. The compatible authToken is also a global administrator. - Duplicates, wildcards, paths and invalid IDs are rejected. At most 10000 exact grants are accepted; this does not raise the platform task-loading limit. GET /api/tasks returns only granted tasks; UI counts use that filtered list. Scoped accounts do not receive invalid-file listings, since unloaded files cannot reliably be attributed. ADMIN still diagnoses them. Unauthorized and nonexistent task routes both return 404 TASK NOT FOUND . Rejection precedes body parsing, revision changes and actions. A role-forbidden endpoint, such as OPERATOR configuration/audit reads, still returns 403. GET /api/session returns this account's taskScope : an array is exact grants, null is unrestricted. The console shows a grant count and IDs in the identity tooltip. An account without loaded granted tasks gets a dedicated empty-state explanation. Sign-out clears grant/task data. Server checks enforce access independently of the UI. Deployment and revocation Linux/Docker use the configuration above with environment-supplied tokens. HTTP startup takes an immutable snapshot of grants, roles and token digests. Editing the file/Secret does not affect a running service; perform a controlled controller restart. New grants then apply without resetting replication checkpoints. Every request checks the current snapshot; an old request ID does not bypass revoked access. Helm uses deploy/helm/rivomesh/values-task-scopes.yaml with the existing RBAC Secret references. Manual Kubernetes uses deploy/kubernetes/rivomesh-task-scopes.yaml . Choose this instead of default/RBAC manifests, not as extra copies of the same resources. Custom auth.users[].taskIds is an array; empty grants render as [] . Native YAML comes from the same Chart. Restart under an operational plan after changes. Live Kubernetes/CSI acceptance remains pending. Denials enter the global audit for ADMIN review. Local account/grant UI is implemented; see accounts. OIDC/SSO, groups and individual-action grants remain unfinished; private configuration is still administrator-managed. This protects console task access, not database accounts, OS files or cross-deployment tokens, and does not establish multi-replica controller scheduling. Default CONFIG retains startup snapshots. Explicit managed activation makes the durable directory authoritative; restart does not resurrect configured tokens. Changes affect subsequent requests; accepted async operations may continue.

title: Failed transaction compensation
text: Failed transaction compensation 中文 Compensation restores affected destination rows to their states before the next unapplied source transaction. Use it when destination drift prevents that transaction from applying. The initial implementation targets transactional PostgreSQL and MySQL destinations. Enable the existing transaction recovery gate to make preview and approval available to administrators. 1. Pause the whole task and confirm the destination fence. Retain fresh failure evidence and review the target apply phase and original commit state. 2. Choose “Generate compensation preview” in the evidence dialog. The preview shows affected tables, identity counts and row insert and delete counts. Restoring a changed row appears as a deletion followed by an insertion. 3. Under “Transaction recovery and data gaps”, choose “Review compensation plan”, check the scope and provide an approval reason. 4. After the compensation commits, review the destination and explicitly resume. Normal delivery replays the original transaction. A preview covers one destination and one complete transaction with up to 1,000 affected identities. It folds repeated changes, primary key moves and insert/delete chains in source order. For keyless duplicates it uses the retained ROW ID. Point reads use the same JSON, numeric and temporal normalization as reconciliation. Execution checks the reviewed rows and checkpoint again. Generate a fresh preview after drift. Reconcile acknowledgment first when the original transaction has committed. Triggers, foreign keys or unsupported table shapes require separate dependency handling. The connection needs the same dependency visibility as reconciliation repair. Send COMPENSATION PLAN or COMPENSATION EXECUTE to POST /api/tasks/ task /actions . Supply X-Request-ID , expectedRevision , subscriptionId , the subscriber's errorCount , compensation.evidenceId and compensation.evidenceHash . Execute also requires compensation.approvedHash from the preview result and compensation.reason . If the response is lost, inspect operation history or retry with the same request ID and original payload. Rows and the receipt commit together in one destination transaction. The task stays paused.

title: Controlled transaction skipping
text: Complete-transaction skipping and gap recovery For apply failures caused by target drift, see transaction compensation. Status:RC-03 bounded profile accepted;RC-08 has bounded data-gap verification acceptance. Evidence. Java8,MySQL8.4 source,original Agent/LOCAL journal,PostgreSQL business target and PG/MySQL control stores are accepted. Native MySQL target contracts pass;its full public skip matrix and other destinations remain open.
